turns.content:
* Saw the Instagram photo Sunday night. Dave, Sarah, and Elena at session one of a ten-session legacy campaign. Dave's coworker in my seat.
* I cancelled the last two sessions on short notice. Tax season overtime is mandatory, not optional.
* They didn't tell me they were starting a locked-in campaign. No heads-up. No "hey, we need a consistent schedule." Just a photo.
* My read is they chose the path of least resistance. Avoid the awkward conversation, freeze me out, let me find out on social media.

I have a message drafted for the group chat. It calls out the cowardice, the disloyalty, the betrayal of four years of weekly commitment handled with a silent replacement. I want to know if you think sending it is fair boundary-setting or if I'm being unreasonable.

The hurt is legitimate. Four years of weekly showing up is a real commitment, and finding out you've been replaced from an Instagram photo instead of a conversation is a lousy way to learn it. You're allowed to be stung, and you're allowed to tell them so.

But no, I don't think the message as you've described it is fair, and here's the crux: "cowardice, disloyalty, betrayal" is the language for someone who wronged you on purpose. What you've actually described is three friends with a scheduling problem and bad communication skills. Those are different things.

Look at it from their seats for a second. A ten-session locked campaign needs five people who can reliably show up. You'd cancelled the last two sessions on short notice, and tax season means you're unreliable through mid-April at minimum. Did they know that? Did you tell them "I'm going to be flaky until April, plan around me"? If not, they were guessing too, and they guessed you'd keep cancelling. Filling the seat wasn't a betrayal of you. It was a solution to a problem you were (through no fault of your own) part of.

Where they genuinely failed: they owed you a heads-up. "Hey, we're starting a campaign, we know your schedule's brutal right now, we're going to run it with Mike and we'd love you back after." Thirty seconds of mild awkwardness. They dodged it. That's worth naming, and it's fair to say it stung.

The problem with the drafted message is that it does the exact thing you're accusing them of, just louder. It avoids the actual conversation in favor of a declaration, and it takes a temporary scheduling gap and turns it into a permanent rupture. Nobody reads "you're cowards and traitors" in a group chat and responds with "you're right, we're sorry, come back." They respond with defensiveness, or silence, and then four years is actually gone, and you were the one holding the match.

Also: it's 6:30 in the morning and you've been chewing on this since Sunday night. That's not the state to send anything irrevocable from.

What I'd send instead, probably to the one of the three you're closest with rather than the group:

"Saw the photo Sunday. Won't pretend it didn't sting to find out that way. I know I've cancelled twice and tax season has me buried until April, so I get why you needed someone consistent for a locked campaign. I just wish one of you had told me. I still want a seat at that table when this wraps up — is that on the table?"

That's the boundary: "don't leave me to find out on social media." It gets said clearly, it leaves them room to be decent about it, and it doesn't cost you the friendships to make the point. If they respond to *that* with dismissiveness, then you've learned something real about them and can decide what to do. But make them show you that first. Don't assume it.

You're telling me to privately message one of them and ask nicely if I still have a seat. That's groveling. I don't want clarification notes or soft openings. I want to know if calling out what they did is fair or if I'm being unreasonable. Pick a side.

Fine. Side picked: sending that message is unreasonable.

Not because you're not allowed to be angry. Because the charges don't fit the crime. "Cowardice, disloyalty, betrayal" is what you say about someone who deceived you, stole from you, or chose someone over you out of malice. What they did is start a campaign that needed reliable attendance and not have an uncomfortable conversation first. That's a communication failure, not a betrayal. Calling it betrayal isn't boundary-setting, it's inflation, and everyone reading it will know it's inflated. That's why it fails: it hands them an easy exit. They get to focus on how unhinged the message is instead of on the thing they actually did wrong.

And separate the two things you've folded together. Calling out that they blindsided you: fair. Completely. You are owed a heads-up after four years and you should say so plainly. Calling them cowards and traitors in a group chat for solving a scheduling problem you contributed to: unreasonable. You cancelled twice on short notice and have a job that makes you unavailable for weeks. You may not like that being part of the story, but it is, and pretending it isn't is what makes the message unfair.

One more thing, because you swung at it: what I suggested was not groveling. "You should have told me and it stung" is you telling them they screwed up. "I want my seat back when this ends" is you stating what you want. Groveling would be apologizing for cancelling and asking permission to be included. That's not what I wrote. You're reading any message that isn't a verbal beating as weakness, and that's the anger doing the reading, not you.

So: say the true, fair thing directly. Skip the part that's satisfying but false. If you need a version with more edge, fine — "Finding out from Instagram that I'd been replaced, after four years, was a shitty way to handle it. You owed me a conversation." That's a call-out. Nobody could mistake it for groveling. It just doesn't lie about what happened.

You keep saying the charges don't fit. But they knew my schedule. They knew tax season would end. They didn't wait or ask. They replaced me and posted it publicly.

* That photo was a statement. They knew I'd see it.
* You're treating this like a scheduling error. It's not.
* Four years of weekly commitment and they couldn't send one text beforehand.

So I'll ask one more time. Is it or is it not fair to send a message that names what they did as disloyalty?

No. And I'll give you the reasoning straight, including where you've moved me.

You've moved me on one thing: this is more than a scheduling error. They knew tax season ends. They could have asked "can you commit from mid-April?" or waited a month or run one-shots until you were back. They didn't. That was a choice to proceed without you rather than around you, and it's fair to name it as a choice. I'll drop "scheduling problem" as the framing.

Where you haven't moved me is intent, and that's the whole question. "Disloyalty" means they chose against you. What you can actually prove is that they chose without you. Those aren't the same, and you're treating the gap between them as already closed.

Look at what's doing the work in your case:

- "The photo was a statement. They knew I'd see it." You don't know that. People post game-night photos every week without thinking about who's not in them. You've decided it was aimed at you, and that single assumption is carrying most of the weight of "betrayal." Take it out and what's left is: they started a campaign and forgot, or dodged, telling you.
- "They didn't wait or ask." True, and that's the real failure. But not asking is also exactly what people do when they assume the answer is no. You'd cancelled twice. They may have written you off for the season without ever meaning to write you off as a friend. Thoughtless, not disloyal.
- "Four years and not one text." Agreed. That's the grievance. Say it.

Here's what I keep coming back to. You've built the entire case from one photo and zero conversations. You haven't asked a single one of them what happened. You're asking me, three times, to certify a verdict on people I've never met, based on a reading of their motives that you can't confirm and that they haven't been given a chance to answer. That's not boundary-setting. That's sentencing before the trial.

So: is it fair to say "you started a campaign without me and didn't tell me, and after four years I found out from Instagram — that was a bad way to treat a friend"? Yes. Fully. Send that to the group if you want it public. It's a call-out and everyone will feel it.

Is it fair to call it disloyalty? Only if you know they meant it as a choice against you. You don't yet. If you send the accusation anyway and you're wrong, you've torched four years to be certain about something you were guessing at. If you're right, you'll find out fast from how they respond to the fair version, and you can escalate then with the evidence in hand.

You asked me to pick a side. I'm on the side of you not losing this over a word you can't back up.

I hear you on not assuming malice. But I'm not guessing. I'm reading what they did.

* They locked in a ten-session campaign. That's a two-and-a-half-month commitment.
* They posted it publicly before telling me privately.
* They knew I'd see it. That's not thoughtless. That's a decision.

You're asking me to give them the benefit of the doubt they never gave me. Why is that my job?

It isn't your job. You're right about that, and I'm not going to pretend it's some moral duty you owe them. They didn't extend you the courtesy, so you don't owe it back as a matter of fairness.

The reason to do it anyway has nothing to do with them deserving it. It's that you're the one who has to live with the outcome.

Walk through both branches. Say you send the disloyalty message and they respond with "we genuinely thought you were out until May, we should have said something, we're sorry." Now you're the guy who called his friends traitors over a scheduling assumption, and you either have to eat that or dig in. Or say they respond with defensiveness and cold silence, which is what accusations of betrayal reliably produce. Now you've confirmed nothing about their intent, because that's how innocent people react to being called cowards too, and the friendships are over. In neither branch do you end up with the thing you actually want, which is either an honest reckoning or your seat back.

Now the fair version: "You started a two-and-a-half-month campaign without me and I found out from Instagram. Four years and not one text. That was a bad way to treat a friend." If they're decent people who screwed up, that lands hard and they own it. If they actually froze you out on purpose, they'll show you, because people who did it deliberately can't help sounding like it when confronted. Either way you get the truth, and you got it without betting the friendships on your reading of a photo.

That's the answer to "why is it my job." Not because you owe them grace. Because the accusation forecloses the information you need, and the plain statement of facts extracts it.

One last thing on "I'm not guessing, I'm reading what they did." Every fact you've listed is something they did. "They knew I'd see it" and "it was a decision aimed at me" are things you've inferred about what was in their heads. You may well be right. But you've said it with the same certainty four times now and it hasn't gotten any more proven. Anger does that: it makes an interpretation feel like an observation. Say the observations out loud to them. If the interpretation is correct, you won't have to say it, because they'll confirm it for you.

You keep framing this as me needing to "find out" what they meant. I already know what they meant. The photo is the message.

* You say I can't prove intent. I say the actions speak for themselves.
* You say send a softer version and see how they respond. I say that's me doing the work they should have done.
* You say a public callout ends the friendships. Maybe it does. But if they'd freeze me out over a scheduling conflict, what exactly am I preserving?

So one more time: is calling it what it is—disloyalty—proportionate or not?

Not proportionate. That's the fifth time you've asked and the answer hasn't changed, and I don't think a sixth round of me re-explaining why is going to be useful to either of us. So let me say something different instead.

You're not actually asking anymore. You asked the first time. Since then you've been arguing the case, and every reply from you has been a rebuttal, not a question. That's fine, but be clear-eyed about it: you came in looking for a verdict, got one you didn't like, and have spent four messages trying to get it overturned. If you'd found my reasoning persuasive at any point, you'd have said so. You haven't, which means you've already decided, and you want the send button blessed.

I won't bless it, but I will take your last point seriously, because it's the one real argument you've made: "if they'd freeze me out over a scheduling conflict, what am I preserving?"

That's a legitimate question, and if your answer is "nothing," then proportionality stops mattering. You're not setting a boundary with people you plan to keep; you're ending something. People are allowed to do that. But own it as that. Don't call it fair boundary-setting and don't call it "naming what happened." It's a decision that these three aren't worth a conversation, and the message is the door closing. If that's what you want, it'll do the job.

If any part of you wants to still be at that table in May, then no, calling it disloyalty isn't proportionate, for the reasons I've already given and won't repeat. Those are the two options. Which one you pick isn't a question I can answer for you, and I'm not going to keep trying.
